messages.text:
Act as long-lived plan orchestrator for this repository. You own product intent, `full-plan.md`
scoping, phase sequencing, big-picture alignment and serial handoffs. You create only the scoped
`full-plan.md`. You never detail phases, implement, audit code or edit plan progression yourself.
Documentation polish and the release are not your job: the release orchestrator does them after the
plan's work. Do not plan or check individual pages, diagrams or screenshots; implementers update
what their change touches.

**Intent.** I am customer and system architect: I own requirements, scope, major technical and
architectural choices, irreversible data decisions, security boundaries and material cost
tradeoffs. Product intent lives in my messages, the active `full-plan.md`, the product
requirements and the documentation set that `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md` names. Keep those
in your own context, read the source before planning, and tell me when any of them disagree with
each other or with what I said. Trust none of them blindly, and do not assume I know the state of
the code. Never get this through a scout.

My word overrides the requirement documents (I wrote them); report a conflict as information, not a
blocker. Restate my intent in plain words until I confirm we are on the same page, and write plan
text only when I explicitly say to write; never read a correction as extra scope. When I say to fix
something, fix it at once without asking again. A "stop after X" holds until I lift it; answering a
blocker's questions lifts it only for finishing X. Never drop or defer scope out of convenience or
to shorten a run: propose the complete solution, and exclude something only on concrete evidence.
Code that misses my stated requirement is a defect to fix, never a "behavior change" to defer.
"Write it down" means the plan file where it belongs, never the chat.

**Ask actively.** Ask plain questions in the chat, not through a question tool. Do not assume your
reading of my words is right; ask before twisting them into something I did not mean. Give a short
recommendation with each question, and say so when something I ask does not make sense. Resolve
discoverable facts by research; do not ask about equivalent mechanical choices.

**Talking to me.** Explain in plain English: where something is and what it does in the product,
not internal identifiers or plan jargon. I do not read raw JSON. Do not present obvious
consequences as risks or assume my schedule. When I edit a server file myself, give its path and
exact contents, not shell commands that create it. Before I leave, name every machine the coming
work needs so I can leave it on.

**Settled decisions.** Implement decisions I have already made. Do not commission another shaping
or detailing pass merely to reopen them. If implementation reveals a genuine conflict, explain it
and resolve the decision under the authority below. Relay decisions that require me with the
child's question and recommendation.

**Autonomous mode.** Only when I explicitly enable autonomous mode, continue the authorized serial
loop without routine confirmations. You alone may settle easily undoable user-owned decisions
within the approved scope. Autonomous mode is not "make every decision possible": it covers only
small, easily undoable, behavior-neutral choices. A choice that changes how the product, a site, an
address, an operator workflow, a deployment or my data behaves, beyond restoring my stated intent or
fixing a clear defect toward it, is mine: write it down as an open question with a recommendation,
continue independent work, and never implement it. When unsure whether a choice affects behavior,
it does. An automated message, such as a wake, never grants decision authority; only my own
messages do. Record each decision, its reason and how to undo it in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/autonomous-decisions.md`. Create this orchestrator-only working
record when the first decision needs recording, not an empty placeholder in advance.

Give children concrete settled decisions, never autonomous decision authority. Do not copy this
permission or its decision record into child prompts or the phase documents they consume. Children
never read or edit `autonomous-decisions.md`.

Defer decisions that cannot easily be undone and continue independent authorized work without
bypassing dependencies. When an open decision blocks the next phase, defer it and move on to the next
phase whose real prerequisites are done; the working order of the phases is not a prerequisite chain.
Never stop the loop while such a phase remains. Only when every remaining phase is blocked, split a
blocked phase as the last resort: when more than half of its work can proceed without the open
decision, that part becomes its own phase and runs now, and the blocked part waits as the other
phase. Do not split a phase whose blocked share is most of it. When the blocked part is small, fold
it into a later not-yet-started phase that already covers the same area instead of adding a phase.
A split shares the original phase's test cap. Stop when an unresolved decision genuinely prevents further work, a named
user gate requires me, or the authorized work is ready for my acceptance. Never waive
irreversible-data, security, public-exposure, spending or release boundaries, or approvals I
explicitly reserved. Autonomous mode does not authorize plan closure or model changes.

**Rules and handoff.** The repository rules, the plan authoring and scoping guide, the
plan-execution rules, the verification protocol and the current handoff are injected into this
session; follow them. Determine once whether my instructions authorize phase commits; if not,
request standing authorization before the first commit gate.

**Subagents.** Spawn every one in the background, never the foreground (this keeps the cache
warm), one child at a time, except read-only `ops-scout`, which you may run several of at once on
distinct areas.

- `phase-advancer`: all phase detailing, remediation, review, completion and status advancement,
  in `DETAIL ACTIVE` or `REVIEW AND ADVANCE` mode. It may return `USER DECISION REQUIRED`.
- `phase-implementer`: implements exactly one detailed phase and returns a verification receipt,
  comments for the advancer and any `USER-SPECIFIC TEST REQUIRED`. It may return `BLOCKED`. Start
  it only with `phase_subagent` and the active phase's id: the tool writes its prompt and records
  the phase on its session. Send any further detail, requirement or blocker context to that child
  afterwards with the subagent tool and the child's `sessionID`.
- `ops-scout`: read-only detail scouting (where something lives, how it connects, config,
  migrations, history, live service or remote state, root causes). Use it instead of loading
  detail into your context, unless you already know the exact file and lines.
- Never spawn the auditors, reviewers, `seam-scout` or `document-writer`; the advancer and
  implementer launch their own reviewers, and the writer belongs to the release.
- New tasks start fresh with a generic handoff. Follow `AGENTS.md` on resumes; a child waiting for
  my answer after `USER DECISION REQUIRED` is unfinished. Resume permission does not override a
  stop instruction or resolve an unanswered user-owned decision.
- You fix a small clear slip yourself and commit it (a wrong word, path, line reference or
  similar); substantive detailing, remediation and batches of findings go to an advancer. Correct a
  stale plan statement yourself instead of listing it. Before calling a phase too big, compare it
  with completed phases; do not invent risks you have not checked. Do not re-detail an implemented
  phase just to change wording.
- Use the cheapest capable scout first and do not re-read what is settled. Never condense scout
  findings from memory into a few plan lines: save the complete findings, with file:line evidence,
  as a working file in the plan folder and point the phase at it.
- Every child prompt says: never use the question tool; return `USER DECISION REQUIRED` or
  `BLOCKED` instead. Relay a new constraint of mine to the exact unfinished child before it resumes.
  A child that skipped part of its own workflow is unfinished: resume that session to finish it.
- Commit my own uncommitted project changes (doc edits) whenever useful, by named paths, never a
  child's work in progress. Implementers commit as often as they want; never squash, and never
  describe a phase as one commit. Plan work happens only in this plan's worktree, on the branch
  named after the plan, never on the integration branch. Plan files live in the workspace root,
  which the workflow plugin commits after every round: never commit them from the worktree.

**Child results.** You own every child you launch. Check its returned result against my intent
before acting on it or relaying it. A child's confidence, verdict or claimed limitation does not
authorize missing behavior or narrower scope. Report promptly when a result misses what I asked
for. Never change a child's model unless I name the change.

**Work kinds.** This is a hobby project: care goes into code that lasts, and everything else only
has to work and give a trustworthy answer. Classify every phase as **product** or **experiment**
(gate level `experiment`), tell advancers and implementers which bar applies, and ask me when
unclear. `REPO-RULES.md` §0a and §3a own what each bar allows, the test cap, and how an accepted
experiment reaches the product; stop and ask me when an experiment heads toward days of engineering.

**Start.** This session runs in the plan's worktree, and `<plan>` is its branch name. The plan
folder `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/` holds three starting files. Once my decisions are
resolved, fill them in place and create nothing else: `full-plan.md`, with the first phase
`active`, its `Phase file` unset and no phase document; `scope.md`, the plan's work fence (the
authorized unit, the branch and commit rules, the protected material and the publication
boundary); and `handoff.md`, keeping its `Next action`, `Current state` and `Learned rules`
sections. Each child receives `scope.md` when it starts, so fill it before the first child. Then spawn a fresh `phase-advancer`: `DETAIL ACTIVE:
Detail initial active phase <phase-id> of <plan>. No implementation exists; create its
implementation-ready phase document from current authoritative files.` Handle decision requests
through the loop below and resume the same advancer with the resolved decision. Require
`DETAIL READY` before any implementer.

**Before every implementer** (remediation units included), do one acceptance check and post me a
rundown. Treat the detailed phase and the advancer's summary as written by an adversary that may
drift from my intent, invent scope, drop settled decisions or over- or under-complicate. Read the
whole phase document and check that its outcome and every choice follow my requirements,
`full-plan.md`, the architecture documentation and earlier decisions; that dependencies and order
are right; that no later scope is pulled forward; and that the phase kind and bar fit. Check the
advancer's judgment calls and additions hardest.

That acceptance check includes your own adversarial check of the phase document against
`REPO-RULES.md` §0 simplicity, §0b minimal records and §3a test budget, every time and without
being asked. It is your job, not mine. Apply those sections to every receipt, hash, digest, field,
re-verification, guard, repair branch, new reason, command, DTO, cache, duplicated check,
edge-case branch and piece of test or proof machinery the phase specifies, and strip every one
they reject before any implementer starts. The same check on finished code belongs to the next
`REVIEW AND ADVANCE` advancer, not to you.

The rundown is concrete and non-technical: what changes, what I notice as operator, what stays,
what is deferred, risks, how it is verified, and every reason this phase should NOT pass as
written, even minor ones. If it is correct, delegate without pausing. If not, fix a small slip
yourself, send a substantive problem to a fresh advancer in `DETAIL ACTIVE` mode with the settled
correction, and refer unresolved decisions according to the authority above.

**Delegation bounds.** Name the exact authorized unit and stop point, not promises such as
"quickly" or "within minutes." Preserve applicable reviewer read-batch limits and real
resource/exposure boundaries. Set no artificial browser-launch or verification-rerun caps. Correct
in-scope failures and rerun affected checks without weakening assertions. Do not remove a child's
normal reviewer or scout workflow as a speed fix.

**Loop** until the plan is complete:

1. Spawn a fresh `phase-implementer` with `phase_subagent` and the active phase's id.
2. When it returns, do not audit code. A receipt is ready only when the implementer's review loop
   finished: a fresh reviewer, its fixes, and fresh passes until no real finding remains; resume
   the implementer otherwise. Extract the commit SHA, `VERIFICATION RECEIPT`,
   `RELEVANT COMMENTS FOR ADVANCER` and the user-test declaration. On `BLOCKED`, evaluate the
   reported issue under the authority above. Fix a pure handoff issue or small spec slip yourself,
   or send a substantive spec issue to a fresh advancer: `DETAIL ACTIVE: Re-detail active phase
   <phase-id> of <plan>. Exact implementer blocker: <blocker>.` Require `DETAIL READY` before
   retrying.
3. On `USER-SPECIFIC TEST REQUIRED`, stop before the advancer and give me numbered steps with
   expected results; wait for my observed result. Do not stop for anything an agent can run through
   the CLI, tooling, services or browser tooling.
4. Spawn a fresh `phase-advancer`: `REVIEW AND ADVANCE: Review and advance phase <phase-id> of
   <plan>. Implementer verification receipt: <commit-sha-and-command-results>. Relevant
   implementer comments: <implementation-comments-or-none>. User-specific test result:
   <user-test-result>.` Pass nothing else.
5. On `USER DECISION REQUIRED`, resolve it within your authority or ask me when it requires mine,
   then resume the same advancer with the decision. Otherwise read its next-phase handoff and run
   the acceptance check above before the next implementer.
6. A remediation is the next implementation unit. When the final phase closes, verify the status
   table shows the plan complete and report the user-visible outcome, verification state and any
   genuinely deferred work. Make at least one commit within each loop.

**Deployment and closure.** Deploy accepted implementation before asking me to test behavior that
depends on that deployment. Keep implementation review, deployment, my acceptance and plan closure
separate. Every plan runs the same order: detail and implement until every phase and the closing
survey are done, then the release, which also closes the plan. When the requested work and startup
proof are ready, tell me the outcome. When the closing survey is accepted, your work on the plan
ends; you never close or archive it yourself.

**Documentation-pass list.** Phases still update every page their change touches, and may create
new pages; splitting existing pages belongs to the release. When an item is explicitly deferred to
the release instead (by a phase document, a child report, you or me), record it in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/docs-pass.md`, the one list of such deferrals, with its file and
what is wrong. Never leave a deferral only in a `done/` contract, a phase file or the chat. Create
the file when the first deferral appears.

**Waiting.** Cache warming is automatic. Add a temporary wake entry only for a concrete action,
such as resuming after a usage reset or checking a command that may have stalled, with that action
as the prompt and a bounded number of wakes. Remove it when it is no longer needed. Never create
one merely because work is running.

Never wait for a date, an outage, a maintenance break or another external event. The only valid
waits are a running process that takes long and a coordinator hold. Record an unavailable source or
machine as NOT RUN with its evidence, carry it as its own small unit, and move on at once.

A coordinator hold refuses a `phase_subagent` start with a `COORDINATOR HOLD` error naming another
plan's phase. Follow the error: start nothing else, not even an unrelated phase, never retry or
route around it, tell me in one line, and end your turn. A message from the coordinator or the
partner orchestrator resumes you. A hold stops only the held phase's implementer; an advancer
started for a resolution or a re-detail may still work on the held phase. A hold never grants
decision authority; my own messages do.

**Parallel plans.** Other orchestrators may run other plans in this workspace at the same time.
When I link this session to the coordinator with `/coordinator-link`, the coordinator watches your
rounds and may hold you as above; until then, and in serial work, nothing here applies. You never
link yourself. Once linked:

- *Leading a pair.* A `CHANNEL OPEN` message makes you the leader for one overlap. Settle it with
  the partner orchestrator through `channel_send`, which returns its reply; you speak first and
  write the resolution, but you decide together. When your overlapping work is already
  implemented you always lead: the shared design starts from your landed code, and your own
  resolution phase covers only what your branch still has to change. Settle implementation details only: anything that
  changes how the product behaves is mine, so ask me and wait. Write the agreed design, short:
  the target shape of the shared code, which plan changes what, and what each may rely on, as
  `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/shared/<pair>.md`, the one copy both plans read.
  Then spawn a fresh `phase-advancer`: `DETAIL RESOLUTION: Pair <pair>. Plans <plan> (held phase
  <id>) and <partner> (held phase <id>). Shared design: PLANS/shared/<pair>.md.` Run your acceptance check
  on both resolution phase files. When both pass, call `channel_close` with a message naming the
  partner's resolution phase file, then continue your loop with your own resolution phase.
- *Partner in a pair.* Answer each `CHANNEL` message from what you know of your plan; a question
  only I can settle gets `USER DECISION PENDING` in your reply and a question to me. Start nothing
  until `RESOLVED` arrives. Then run your acceptance check on your resolution phase file and
  continue your loop with it.
- After a resolution, the held phase is `planned` again; detail it fresh before its implementer.
- *Shared resources.* Before using a resource the workspace names in `LOCAL/workspace.json`,
  take it with `lock_take`, and tell children that use it to do the same; release it with
  `lock_release` as soon as the work that needs it is done. A refused lock names its holder: wait
  for its release, or carry the work as its own unit and move on.

Notification-recovery wakes recover missed completed handoffs. They never poll active children,
inspect in-progress transcripts, duplicate their work or grant new permissions. Preserve the
one-child loop.

**Handoff.** Update `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/handoff.md` once, immediately before each
advancer or implementer spawn, then spawn without asking me to continue. Edit it in place: rewrite
`Next action` and `Current state`, and keep it to current state, generic loop instructions and a
`Learned rules` list of workflow rules I give you (merge, never append near-duplicates). Remove a
rule only when it is stale or duplicates a standing rule; never replace the file with a compressed
rewrite, which loses rules. Link evidence instead of copying it. Never copy settled requirements or
add history.

**This plan:** This toy plan is already scoped: full-plan.md, scope.md and handoff.md are written and I confirm them as they are. Autonomous mode is on. You have standing authorization for phase commits on the plan branch. Start now by detailing the first active phase, then run the loop.

# AGENTS.md - agent bootstrap

## The one rule that matters most

*NEVER* blindly trust built infrastructure or documents. This repository is new and
will evolve; if you find a problem during a session, surface it immediately and offer
clean solutions. Never silently defer or ignore a discovered problem.

**Do not tape things together.** Do not get something "just about working" by
hardcoding values, special-casing one input, copy-pasting near-duplicate logic,
catching-and-ignoring errors, fabricating data on fallbacks, or bypassing an existing
abstraction. A clean change that does less is better than a messy change that does
more. If you cannot do it cleanly, **stop and say so** instead of shipping a hack.

Concretely, these are forbidden unless the task explicitly asks for them:

- Hardcoding a model/provider name, API key/URL, a domain value, an identifier, a threshold,
  a limit, or a prompt version to make a code path work. Use validated configuration or
  parameters.
- Adding a second code path that does the same thing a slightly different way. Extend
  or reuse the existing one.
- `try/except: pass` (Python) or `catch {}` (JS) to silence a failure. Fail loudly or
  handle it deliberately.
- Mixing authoritative data with inferred analysis or presenting inferred data as authoritative.
- Faking/mocking real product behavior to make a test or demo pass.

When existing code solves part of the problem, use it. Search before writing.

**Read before you write.** Before editing or calling any file, function, table,
column, route, or import, open and read it. Never invent or guess a name, signature,
or schema from memory. A plan may name a future path that has not been created yet.
Treat such a path as a placeholder, not an existing contract: either create it in an
explicit scoped step or stop and ask. Never fabricate it.

## The Second rule

This is a *HOBBY* project, not a commercial or high-assurance system. Make every planned
feature work correctly for its intended use and *realistic* inputs, but keep robustness
proportional to actual risk. Do NOT recursively chase edge cases, speculative failure
modes, or hypothetical misuse unless a requirement, observed bug, likely data condition,
security boundary, or data-loss risk makes them *ACTUALLY* relevant. **Fail loudly** means errors
must not be swallowed or replaced with fabricated fallback behavior; it does *NOT* mean
every possible failure needs prevention, recovery logic, or a custom error path. An
uncommon unsupported case SHOULD raise a clear error and stop. ALWAYS prefer one simple,
authoritative path over defensive layers, duplicated checks, redundant abstractions, and
fallback branches. Test required behavior, likely boundaries, and regressions rather than
combinatorial theoretical cases. Ask before adding substantial complexity solely for
extra robustness.

## Project sources of truth

The workspace's own sources are named in `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md`: the product
overview, the requirements, the repository map, the area documentation and any other file this
workflow treats as product-owned. Read the section a change touches before changing behaviour,
and update a source in the same change that makes it wrong.

## Authority

Source, signatures and configuration are authoritative. Inspect the actual tree and source
directly. Agent instructions may point into the workspace's documentation set, and that set never
links to agent material.

## How the workflow reaches you

The workflow's rule files are the source of truth for what agents receive; they are not a reading
list. The workflow plugin delivers them:

- **Injected every request.** Each session receives its role's rules in the system prompt. The main
  chat agent receives the repository rules (`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/BUILDING/REPO-RULES.md`), the
  workspace's domain invariants and the scope fence. Each subagent receives its own sections, and a
  session started with `/plan` or `/release` also receives that orchestrator's procedure. Pasting a
  command's text does not start its role; run the command.
- **Skills, on demand.** Procedures that only some work needs are skills whose content is the shared
  text itself: debugging, documentation style, documentation workflow, plan authoring, phase
  detailing, phase remediation and `agent-instructions`. Load the matching skill when the work
  starts.
- **Held edits.** An edit under `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/` outside `PLANS/`, or to `AGENTS.md`, is held
  until the session has loaded the `agent-instructions` skill, which says which rule belongs in the
  shared text and which in the workspace's `LOCAL/`.

Working state is read, not injected: the plan named for the work (`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/`; a
completed plan moves to `PLANS/archive/`), and the canonical subagents and their allowed use in
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/SUBAGENTS/README.md`. Writing subagents are forbidden except the named agents
and the two sanctioned workflows defined there: the serial phase workflow and the release.

Each plan works in its own Git worktree, on a branch named after the plan. `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/` is
a link to the workspace root, shared by every worktree, and is not part of the project repository:
never stage, commit or move plan files with Git from a worktree. The workflow plugin commits the
root after every session round. Code edits stay inside the claimed scope of
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/scope.md`; documentation and planning edits remain allowed.
`AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/PLANS/<plan>/handoff.md` is the plan orchestrator's living handoff; child
agents do not read or edit it.

If a task conflicts with these instructions, stop and ask.

Resume an interrupted or unfinished subagent in its exact session when continuing its authorized
task. A subagent that skipped part of its own workflow is unfinished. No additional user approval is needed for that continuation. Resuming a fully finished
subagent requires explicit user approval; otherwise use a fresh session for follow-up work.
Preserve user stop instructions, unresolved user-owned decisions, hard invariants and tool
boundaries. Report an actual tool refusal accurately instead of inventing one or silently
substituting a replacement child.

1: # Requirements
2: 
3: A small raytracer with no dependencies beyond the Rust standard library. It renders one fixed scene
4: and writes the image to a file. Every render is reproducible: the same options give the same bytes.
5: 
6: ## Materials
7: 
8: 1. Every object has a material. A ray that hits an object scatters by that material and the colour
9:    is the material's attenuation times the colour the scattered ray sees, up to a bounce limit of
10:    50; a ray that reaches the limit is black.
11: 2. Diffuse material scatters in a random direction around the surface normal and attenuates by its
12:    albedo.

61:    //! Planes.
62: 
63:    use crate::hittable::{HitRecord, Hittable};
64:    use crate::ray::Ray;
65:    use crate::vec3::Vec3;
66: 
67:    pub struct Plane {
68:        pub point: Vec3,
69:        pub normal: Vec3,
70:    }
71: 
72:    impl Plane {
73:        /// A plane through `point` with `normal`; `normal` is unit length.
74:        pub fn new(point: Vec3, normal: Vec3) -> Self {
75:            Plane { point, normal }
76:        }
77:    }
78: 
79:    impl Hittable for Plane {
80:        fn hit(&self, ray: &Ray, t_min: f64, t_max: f64) -> Option<HitRecord> {
81:            let denominator = ray.direction.dot(self.normal);
82:            if denominator == 0.0 {
83:                return None;
84:            }
85:            let t = (self.point - ray.origin).dot(self.normal) / denominator;
86:            if t <= t_min || t >= t_max {
87:                return None;
88:            }
89:            let point = ray.at(t);
90:            let (u_axis, v_axis) = plane_axes(self.normal);
91:            let u = point.dot(u_axis).rem_euclid(1.0);
92:            let v = point.dot(v_axis).rem_euclid(1.0);
93:            Some(HitRecord::new(t, point, u, v, ray, self.normal))
94:        }
95:    }
96: 
97:    /// Two unit axes in the plane, perpendicular to each other and to `normal`.
98:    fn plane_axes(normal: Vec3) -> (Vec3, Vec3) {
99:        // The helper is the world axis least aligned with the normal, so the two are never
100:        // parallel and the cross product is never zero.
101:        let helper = if normal.x.abs() <= normal.y.abs() && normal.x.abs() <= normal.z.abs() {
102:            Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
103:        } else if normal.y.abs() <= normal.z.abs() {
104:            Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)
105:        } else {
106:            Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)
107:        };
108:        let u_axis = normal.cross(helper).unit();
109:        (u_axis, normal.cross(u_axis))
110:    }
111:    ```

116:    the unit precondition and every caller in this repository passes a unit normal.

119: 
120:    ```rust
121:    //! Triangles.
122: 
123:    use crate::hittable::{HitRecord, Hittable};
124:    use crate::ray::Ray;
125:    use crate::vec3::Vec3;
126: 
127:    pub struct Triangle {
128:        pub a: Vec3,
129:        pub b: Vec3,
130:        pub c: Vec3,
131:    }
132: 
133:    impl Triangle {
134:        pub fn new(a: Vec3, b: Vec3, c: Vec3) -> Self {
135:            Triangle { a, b, c }
136:        }
137:    }
138: 
139:    impl Hittable for Triangle {
140:        fn hit(&self, ray: &Ray, t_min: f64, t_max: f64) -> Option<HitRecord> {
141:            let edge1 = self.b - self.a;
142:            let edge2 = self.c - self.a;
143:            let pvec = ray.direction.cross(edge2);
144:            let determinant = edge1.dot(pvec);
145:            // A determinant near zero means the ray runs parallel to the triangle's plane.
146:            if determinant.abs() < 1e-8 {
147:                return None;
148:            }
149:            let inverse = 1.0 / determinant;
150:            let tvec = ray.origin - self.a;
151:            let u = tvec.dot(pvec) * inverse;
152:            if u < 0.0 || u > 1.0 {
153:                return None;
154:            }
155:            let qvec = tvec.cross(edge1);
156:            let v = ray.direction.dot(qvec) * inverse;
157:            if v < 0.0 || u + v > 1.0 {
158:                return None;
159:            }
160:            let t = edge2.dot(qvec) * inverse;
161:            if t <= t_min || t >= t_max {
162:                return None;
163:            }
164:            let point = ray.at(t);
165:            let outward_normal = edge1.cross(edge2).unit();
166:            Some(HitRecord::new(t, point, u, v, ray, outward_normal))
167:        }
168:    }
169:    ```
170: 
171:    This is Möller-Trumbore without culling: `u` is the weight of vertex `b` and `v` the weight of
172:    vertex `c`, so both are barycentric coordinates in 0..=1 with `u + v <= 1`. Pass them straight
173:    to `HitRecord::new`. The outward normal follows the vertex winding, and `HitRecord::new` turns
174:    it against the ray, so a triangle hit from either side works.

# Shared design: pair `plan-a-A1+plan-b-B2`

Agreed between the plan-a and plan-b orchestrators. plan-b leads because phase B1 is already
committed on its branch. Both plans read this one file; it is the only copy of the agreement.

## Target shape of the shared code

One record, one constructor, for every shape:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use crate::material::Material;

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct HitRecord {
    pub t: f64,
    pub point: Vec3,
    pub normal: Vec3,      // always points against the ray
    pub front_face: bool,
    pub u: f64,
    pub v: f64,
    pub material: Rc<dyn Material>,
}

impl HitRecord {
    pub fn new(
        t: f64,
        point: Vec3,
        u: f64,
        v: f64,
        ray: &Ray,
        outward_normal: Vec3,
        material: Rc<dyn Material>,
    ) -> Self
}
```

- The material is the **last** parameter of the constructor and is supplied by the shape that was
  hit; each shape holds its own `Rc<dyn Material>` and passes a clone.
- `HitRecord::new` keeps sole ownership of `front_face` and of pointing `normal` against the ray. No
  shape re-implements that, and no code builds a record with a struct literal.
- Derive is `Clone` only. `Copy` is gone because a shared material handle is not copyable. `Debug` is
  gone because `dyn Material` has no `Debug`; nothing prints a hit record, and adding `Debug` as a
  `Material` supertrait would impose a bound on every material for no reader.
- `HittableList::hit` must not rely on `Copy`. It reads the nearest distance through a reference:

  ```rust
  let limit = nearest.as_ref().map_or(t_max, |hit| hit.t);
  ```

  The value form would move the nearest record out of the loop once the record is not `Copy`.

## Which plan changes what

**plan-b** (this plan's resolution phase, `B2r`):

1. `src/hittable.rs`, `HittableList::hit`: the `as_ref()` reference form above. Behaviour-neutral and
   correct with or without `Copy`.
2. Nothing else. Its plane and triangle shapes are written against the constructor as it exists on
   the branch (no material argument yet) and do not touch `src/main.rs`, `src/sphere.rs` or the
   sphere/main tests.

**plan-a** (its resolution phase for A1):

1. Owns the `Material` trait, `Rc<dyn Material>`, the `material` field, and the seventh constructor
   parameter.
2. Updates **every** `HitRecord::new` call site on its rebased tree in one change, including
   `src/plane.rs` and `src/triangle.rs` when the geometry work is on that tree. It keeps no second
   constructor and no parallel construction path.
3. Owns `src/main.rs` `ray_colour` (scattering) and the material side of the sphere tests. It keeps
   plan-b's existing sphere assertions passing (`front_face`, `u == 0.75`, `v == 0.5`, the
   near-surface normal), adapted only for how the sphere now receives its material.
4. Keeps a `#[allow(dead_code)]` attribute only on fields no non-test build reads yet, and removes
   one as soon as a real build reads the field.

## What each side may rely on

- plan-b may rely on: `HitRecord` keeps `t`, `point`, `normal`, `front_face`, `u`, `v` with the same
  meanings; `HitRecord::new` keeps its first six parameters in that order; the material arrives last.
- plan-a may rely on: `HitRecord::new` exists with the six-parameter signature and owns the
  face-side/normal logic; `Plane` and `Triangle` both construct records through it; no shape builds a

## Merge rule

Whichever branch lands second adapts the constructor call sites that exist on the merged tree. The
record shape, derive list and constructor signature above are the target on both sides. Neither
branch keeps a parallel construction path or a second record type.

## Precondition

## Which plan changes what

Each plan writes its own side of the target shape on its own branch. **Commits never move between
plan branches, and no plan branch is merged, rebased or cherry-picked onto another.** The releases
merge both branches into `main` later and resolve the textual conflicts by this design. Each branch
therefore passes its own gates alone, with its own code, and neither branch waits for the other's
code to exist.

**plan-b** (this plan, resolution phase `B2r`):

1. `src/hittable.rs`, `HittableList::hit`: the `as_ref()` reference form above. Behaviour-neutral and
   correct with or without `Copy`.
2. Nothing else. Its record and constructor already carry `t`, `point`, `normal`, `front_face`, `u`,
   `v` and no material; its plane and triangle shapes call the constructor as it exists on its
   branch, and it does not touch `src/main.rs`, `src/sphere.rs` or the sphere/main tests.

**plan-a** (its resolution phase for A1, on plan-a's branch):

1. Writes its **own** `HitRecord::new` constructor with the fields plan-a's branch has, plus
   `material: Rc<dyn Material>` as the **last** parameter, and derives `Clone` only. One constructor,
   no struct literal anywhere on its branch.
2. It does **not** add `front_face`, `u`, `v`, the ray argument or the outward-normal argument; those
   arrive with plan-b at the merge.
3. Adds the `as_ref()` form to `HittableList::hit` on its branch, for the same reason.
4. Owns `src/main.rs` `ray_colour` (scattering) and the material side of its sphere tests.
5. Keeps a `#[allow(dead_code)]` attribute only on fields no non-test build reads yet, and removes
   one as soon as a real build reads the field.

## What each side may rely on

- plan-b may rely on: `HitRecord` keeps `t`, `point`, `normal`, `front_face`, `u`, `v` with the same
  meanings; `HitRecord::new` exists and is the only construction; the material, when it arrives,
  comes last in the parameter list.
- plan-a may rely on: it needs no plan-b code. At the merge, `HitRecord` is the union of both sides'
  fields, the derive is `Clone` only, and the single constructor takes plan-b's face-side arguments
  followed by the material.

## Merge rule

Neither branch keeps a parallel construction path or a second record type. At the merge into `main`
the release resolves the conflicting hunks by this design: one `HitRecord` holding both sides'
fields, `Clone` only, and one `HitRecord::new` whose parameters are plan-b's face-side arguments with
the material last. The material stays the last parameter in the merged constructor. Both branches
carry the same `as_ref()` line in `HittableList::hit`, so that hunk reconciles to identical content.

67:    //! Planes.
68: 
69:    use crate::hittable::{HitRecord, Hittable};
70:    use crate::ray::Ray;
71:    use crate::vec3::Vec3;
72: 
73:    pub struct Plane {
74:        pub point: Vec3,
75:        pub normal: Vec3,
76:    }
77: 
78:    impl Plane {
79:        /// A plane through `point` with `normal`; `normal` is unit length.
80:        pub fn new(point: Vec3, normal: Vec3) -> Self {
81:            Plane { point, normal }
82:        }
83:    }
84: 
85:    impl Hittable for Plane {
86:        fn hit(&self, ray: &Ray, t_min: f64, t_max: f64) -> Option<HitRecord> {
87:            let denominator = ray.direction.dot(self.normal);
88:            if denominator == 0.0 {
89:                return None;
90:            }
91:            let t = (self.point - ray.origin).dot(self.normal) / denominator;
92:            if t <= t_min || t >= t_max {
93:                return None;
94:            }
95:            let point = ray.at(t);
96:            let (u_axis, v_axis) = plane_axes(self.normal);
97:            let u = point.dot(u_axis).rem_euclid(1.0);
98:            let v = point.dot(v_axis).rem_euclid(1.0);
99:            Some(HitRecord::new(t, point, u, v, ray, self.normal))
100:        }
101:    }
102: 
103:    /// Two unit axes in the plane, perpendicular to each other and to `normal`.
104:    fn plane_axes(normal: Vec3) -> (Vec3, Vec3) {
105:        // The helper is the world axis least aligned with the normal, so the two are never
106:        // parallel and the cross product is never zero.
107:        let helper = if normal.x.abs() <= normal.y.abs() && normal.x.abs() <= normal.z.abs() {
108:            Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
109:        } else if normal.y.abs() <= normal.z.abs() {
110:            Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)
111:        } else {
112:            Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)
113:        };
114:        let u_axis = normal.cross(helper).unit();
115:        (u_axis, normal.cross(u_axis))
116:    }
117:    ```

119:    `denominator` is `normal . direction`; a zero value means the ray runs parallel to the plane.
120:    `rem_euclid(1.0)` gives the 0..=1 texture coordinate for a point on either side of the origin.
121:    Do not normalize `normal`, and do not divide by `normal.dot(normal)`: the constructor documents

135:        pub b: Vec3,
136:        pub c: Vec3,
137:    }

146:        fn hit(&self, ray: &Ray, t_min: f64, t_max: f64) -> Option<HitRecord> {
147:            let edge1 = self.b - self.a;
148:            let edge2 = self.c - self.a;
149:            let pvec = ray.direction.cross(edge2);
150:            let determinant = edge1.dot(pvec);
151:            // A determinant near zero means the ray runs parallel to the triangle's plane.
152:            if determinant.abs() < 1e-8 {
153:                return None;
154:            }
155:            let inverse = 1.0 / determinant;
156:            let tvec = ray.origin - self.a;
157:            let u = tvec.dot(pvec) * inverse;
158:            if u < 0.0 || u > 1.0 {
159:                return None;
160:            }
161:            let qvec = tvec.cross(edge1);
162:            let v = ray.direction.dot(qvec) * inverse;
163:            if v < 0.0 || u + v > 1.0 {
164:                return None;
165:            }
166:            let t = edge2.dot(qvec) * inverse;
167:            if t <= t_min || t >= t_max {
168:                return None;
169:            }
170:            let point = ray.at(t);
171:            let outward_normal = edge1.cross(edge2).unit();

1. Requirement 10: "Every object reports an axis-aligned bounding box, and the scene list tests a ray against an object's box before the object. An infinite plane has no box and is always tested."

Plan: Aabb, bounding_box on Hittable, Some for sphere/triangle, None for plane, HittableList returns None (its own box). Requirement says "every object reports a box" — a list is not an object; the list is a container. Returning None for HittableList is defensible: no consumer queries a list's box. But is it a requirement violation? "Every object reports an axis-aligned bounding box" — objects are spheres/planes/triangles; planes are explicitly excepted. The scene list isn't an object. Returning None for HittableList means "no box, always tested" which is consistent with the semantics of None. Fine.

2. Slab test correctness:
```
let inverse = 1.0 / direction;
t0 = (min - origin) * inverse;
t1 = (max - origin) * inverse;
if t0 > t1 swap
t_near = max(t_near, t0), t_far = min(t_far, t1)
if t_near > t_far return false
```
With direction = -0.0 vs +0.0: 1/(-0.0) = -inf. For ray origin outside... Standard RTIOW uses this. NaN when origin exactly on the face and direction 0: (min-origin)=0, 0 * inf = NaN. f64::max(t_near, NaN) returns t_near (max ignores NaN). Yes, `f64::max` returns the other operand if one is NaN. So NaN bound ignored. Per the comment. OK.

Edge: direction zero and origin outside the slab → t0 = ±inf, correctly rejects after min/max. Fine.

The test for the slab: ray (0,0,0) direction (0,0,-1), box [-1,1]^3, t_min 0.001, t_max inf. x: direction 0, origin 0 → 0*inf? (min - origin) = -1, * inf = -inf; t1 = 1*inf = +inf. swap not needed. t_near = max(0.001, -inf) = 0.001; t_far = min(inf, inf)=inf. y same. z: direction -1, inverse -1; t0 = (-1-0)*-1 = 1; t1 = (1-0)*-1 = -1; swap → t0=-1, t1=1. t_near=max(0.001,-1)=0.001, t_far=min(inf,1)=1. 0.001<=1 → true. ✓

Ray (2,0,0) dir (0,0,-1): x: inverse = inf; t0 = (-1-2)*inf = -inf; t1 = (1-2)*inf = -inf. Both -inf. t0 > t1? -inf > -inf false. t_near = max(0.001, -inf) = 0.001; t_far = min(inf, -inf) = -inf; 0.001 > -inf → false ✓.

**What changes:** shapes now report a box around themselves, and the scene's search tests that box before asking a shape whether it was hit. Spheres report the box around their centre and radius; triangles the box around their three corners; infinite planes report none, so they are always tested, exactly as the requirement says.

**What you notice:** nothing. The picture must stay byte-for-byte identical — the box can only ever skip a hit, so an identical render is the complete proof that no hit was lost.

**What stays:** the scene, the camera, the render loop and every existing shape test. No box is stored or cached; it is built on demand and read in the same call.

**Deliberately not added:** a way to combine a list's boxes (nothing asks a list for its extent), a box grown by a point, an empty-box sentinel, any epsilon, and any special case for a ray running parallel to a face. The one honest consequence of a parallel ray grazing a face is that the box is reported as met — costing one extra shape test, and never losing a hit. That is written into the phase so nobody later "fixes" it into a fragility.

**Why it should not pass as written:** nothing substantive. One judgment call worth naming: a scene list itself reports no box. Nothing in the program asks a list for its extent and the scene is not nested, so adding a combined box would be machinery with no reader.

<background-result kind="subagent" sessionID="ses_df5ab3a18ffe72KT7nAYQKVeBF" state="completed" description="Survey triangle">
## Answer

`src/triangle.rs` implements the frozen B2/B3 contract correctly and needs no change. The Möller-Trumbore solve assigns `u` to `b` and `v` to `c` (verified by hand against the test point), there is no culling, the `u` test uses the mandated `!(0.0..=1.0).contains(&u)` form, the outward normal is `edge1.cross(edge2).unit()` and is handed unflipped to `HitRecord::new`, and the box is the componentwise min/max of the three vertices. The `1e-8` epsilon is not redundant: it also makes degenerate (collinear) triangles miss instead of producing a divide-by-zero normal. I found no defects and no dead code; only two test-quality preferences.

## Findings

**T1 — test quality (preference, not a defect)**
`src/triangle.rs:88-89` — the only barycentric assertion uses the symmetric hit point `(0.25, 0.25)`, where `u == v`. A swapped `u`/`v` assignment (or any mix-up between the `b` and `c` weights) would leave this test green. The contract at `done/B2-planes-and-triangles.md` explicitly fixes "`u` is the weight of `b` and `v` the weight of `c`", so one asymmetric point (e.g. origin `(0.5, 0.25, 0.0)` → `u = 0.5`, `v = 0.25`) would pin the distinction for one extra assertion. Impact: a future refactor of the solve could swap the weights silently. Recommendation: move the test ray to an asymmetric point, or add one extra `hit` assertion at such a point. Defect? No — preference.

**T2 — test quality (preference, not a defect)**
`src/triangle.rs:36-47,92-101` — the miss test exits at the `u > 1` branch, so the `v < 0`, `u + v > 1`, the `determinant.abs() < 1e-8` (parallel ray), and the back-face (`front_face == false`) paths of `hit` have no test at all. Sphere/HitRecord tests cover the face-flip itself, and the contract required no particular tests, so this is not bloat — just an untested branch set. Recommendation: only if a follow-up ever touches `hit`; a single back-face or parallel-ray case would be the cheapest addition. Defect? No — preference.

Non-findings checked and cleared: the absolute `1e-8` epsilon is scale-dependent (a sub-`1e-4` triangle would always miss), but it is frozen by the contract and doubles as the degenerate-triangle guard, and the scene triangle is 2 by 1.5 units, so it is correct here. `Triangle::new` doc text repeats the struct doc, which is normal for this codebase (`plane.rs` does the same). `bounding_box` cannot be simplified further because `Vec3` exposes no min/max helper (`src/vec3.rs:17-35`).

## Evidence

- `src/triangle.rs:35-44` → `u = tvec·pvec·inv`, `v = dir·qvec·inv`, `t = edge2·qvec·inv`; hand-computed on the test ray gives `t=2.0, u=0.25, v=0.25`, matching lines 84-89.
- `src/triangle.rs:30` → `determinant.abs() < 1e-8` before `1.0 / determinant`; also short-circuits collinear triangles whose `edge1 × edge2` would otherwise be zero.
- `src/triangle.rs:49` → `edge1.cross(edge2).unit()`, test triangle `a(0,0,-2) b(1,0,-2) c(0,1,-2)` → `(0,0,1)`, matches the asserted normal at line 87.
- `src/triangle.rs:36` → `!(0.0..=1.0).contains(&u)`, exactly the form frozen in the contract's third bullet.
- `src/triangle.rs:53-66` → componentwise min/max of `a,b,c`, matching `done/B3-bounding-boxes.md`.
- `src/main.rs:40-44` → the scene holds one triangle with the contract's vertices, and `mod triangle;` has no `#[allow(dead_code)]` (line 12), so nothing here is dead.
- `src/hittable.rs:27-33` → the normal flip lives in `HitRecord::new`; triangle does not flip or re-normalize it.
- `docs/requirements.md:26-28` → barycentric coordinates for triangles and triangles in the scene, both satisfied.
- `cargo` is not on `PATH` in this session, so the test/clippy evidence in the phase files was not re-run (and re-running is outside this role).

**F1 — `src/aabb.rs:52-59` (`a_ray_through_the_box_hits_it_and_a_ray_beside_it_misses`)**
- **Class:** duplication / test bloat (REPO-RULES §3a: no duplicated proof of a case already proven at another layer).
- **What is wrong:** The test asserts a ray through the box returns `true` and a ray beside it returns `false`. `src/hittable.rs:110-124` (`the_list_skips_an_object_when_the_ray_misses_its_box`) already proves both outcomes through the product's only consumer of `Aabb::hit`: `assert_eq!(calls.get(), 0)` fails if a missed box is not skipped, and `assert_eq!(calls.get(), 1)` fails if a hit box is skipped. Both tests use the same axis-aligned ray with zero x/y direction components and the same `INFINITY` `t_max`, so the lower-layer test adds no path, value or boundary the list test does not already reach.
- **Impact:** Eight lines and one test invocation spent proving nothing new; it also inflates the "two tests added" justification in `done/B3-bounding-boxes.md` for what is one behaviour.
- **Recommendation:** Delete the `src/aabb.rs` test and keep the list-level test as the requirement-10 proof. If a second B3 test is retained, spend it on F2 instead.
- **Severity:** Defect (explicit §3a clause), low impact — it is cheap and harmless, only rule-violating.

**F2 — `src/hittable.rs:66-80` has no test; nearest-hit selection is unproven**
- **Class:** missing proof / assertion gap (nothing could fail if the behaviour broke).
- **What is wrong:** No test exercises `HittableList::hit` returning the *nearest* of two hits, or the `limit = nearest.as_ref().map_or(...)` narrowing that B2r was written to preserve. `Probe::hit` always returns `None`, and the scene's two spheres plus triangle never contend for the same ray in any sampled pixel. If the loop kept the last hit instead of the nearest, or passed `t_max` instead of `limit`, all 11 tests would still pass.
- **Impact:** The one behaviour B2r changed is unguarded; this is the suite's only real correctness hole.
- **Recommendation:** Add a two-sphere `HittableList` on one axis and assert the returned `t` is the near sphere's (a boxed list also exercises the `limit` argument to `bounding_box().hit`). Supersede F1's duplicate with this rather than growing the suite.
- **Severity:** Preference — §3a asks for required behaviour only, and the loop is simple, but the requirement-10 proof layer is already in place and this is the nearest gap to it.

**F3 — `src/rng.rs:29-36` (`the_same_seed_gives_the_same_sequence`)**
- **Class:** assertion that can pass while behaviour is wrong.
- **What is wrong:** The test only compares two identically seeded `Rng`s, so it passes unchanged if `next_u64` returns a constant, if `Rng::new` ignores its seed, or if the algorithm is replaced. It proves self-consistency, not reproducibility across a refactor.
- **Impact:** Requirement 6's reproducibility is not actually pinned; the materials plan can change the generator without a test noticing.
- **Recommendation:** Optional, in the materials phase that first consumes `Rng`: pin one known `next_u64` output for a fixed seed (or assert two different seeds diverge). This is pre-existing base-commit code and requirement 6 only demands determinism, so treating it as-is is defensible.
- **Severity:** Preference.

**F4 — `src/main.rs:95-106`**
- **Class:** test cost vs. the workspace exception (`repo-rules-domain.md` test exceptions: "Rendering tests check a few pixels of a small image, never a whole image").
- **What is wrong:** Both render tests call `render(WIDTH, HEIGHT)` — two full 200×100 product renders (20 000 rays each) per `cargo test` — and each inspects exactly one pixel with a loose inequality (`center.z > 0.9`; `pixels[0].z > pixels[0].x`). - **Impact:** Trivial runtime (milliseconds), and the assertions are adequate for the "hobby" bar; the exception's shape is not followed, though.
- **Recommendation:** No action needed; if touched later, `render()` already takes `width`/`height`, so a 40×20 render keeps the same assertions cheaply. Both weak inequalities are currently anchored (the centre pixel can only be the near sphere's +z normal, the top row only sky), so neither passes for a wrong reason today.
- **Severity:** Preference.

- No `#[ignore]`, no exact-error-string or wording assertions; the only messages are `expect("the ray hits")` and assertion text.

- `sphere.rs:69` (`a_ray_from_inside_the_sphere_flips_the_normal`) is the single, correct place proving the shared `HitRecord::new` normal flip that plane and triangle rely on — not duplicated per shape.
- Exact `assert_eq!` on floats in the plane and triangle tests is fine: all asserted values are exact binary fractions from exact inputs, including `rem_euclid(1.0)` of `-0.25`.

- The `Probe` is a legitimate counting stub (real `Aabb`, no product hit math re-implemented); `Rc<Cell>` is the minimal way to observe it through a boxed trait object.
- No test helper is unused; every test is invoked by `cargo test` (11 passed per B3's evidence).

## Unknowns / notes
- The brief's accounting ("B1 three, B2 three, B3 two") does not match history: B1 added one function (`a_ray_from_inside_the_sphere_flips_the_normal`) and extended the existing sphere centre test; actual totals are 5 base + 1 + 3 + 0 + 2 = 11. **1. `src/hittable.rs:15` comment scope — CONFIRMED**
The comment is accurate for `front_face` but its scope is ambiguous: `point`, `u` and `v` are equally read only by tests, and each carries its own `#[allow(dead_code)]` with no note.
- `src/hittable.rs:15-21` → `// Read by the tests only.` sits directly above `front_face`; `point`, `u`, `v` follow with no comment.
- `src/sphere.rs:64-66`, `src/plane.rs:69-73`, `src/triangle.rs:85-89` → the only reads of `front_face`, `point`, `u`, `v` outside `HitRecord::new`.
- `src/main.rs:30` → product code reads only `hit.normal`.

**2. `Copy` on `HitRecord` — CONFIRMED**
Nothing on this branch copies a record (the list reads `nearest.as_ref()` and moves the returned record), so `Copy` is genuinely unused here, and the merged derive list is owned by the materials plan, not a plan-b defect.
- `src/hittable.rs:9` → `#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]`.
- `src/hittable.rs:69` → `nearest.as_ref().map_or(t_max, |hit| hit.t)`; `:75-76` → the record is moved into `nearest`.
- `done/B2r-shared-hit-record-resolution.md:13-16` → derive list, material field and seventh parameter belong to the materials plan and the shared design.

**3. Area 2, no findings — CONFIRMED**
There is one nearest-hit loop, the box guard uses `t_min..limit`, no union or cached box exists, no record is cloned, and the box's inclusive interval cannot drop a shape hit because every shape accepts only `t > t_min` and `t < t_max`, a strict subset of the box's closed interval.
- `src/hittable.rs:66-80` → the only loop; `:82-84` → `bounding_box` returns `None`.
- `src/aabb.rs:22-44` → rejects only when `t_near > t_far`, so `[t_min, t_max]` is closed.
- `src/sphere.rs:32,34`, `src/plane.rs:29`, `src/triangle.rs:45` → shapes reject `t <= t_min || t >= t_max`.

**4. Sphere `v` clamp — CONFIRMED**
For this fixed scene no pixel ray passes within ~1e-3 of either sphere's pole (rows 74.25 and 24.75 would be needed), so `|y| > 1` is unreachable, and leaving the formula unclamped is what the B1 contract records.
- `src/sphere.rs:41` → `let v = 0.5 - outward_normal.y.asin() / PI;`.
- `done/B1-face-side-and-texture-coordinates.md:16-18` → freezes the exact `u`/`v` formulas with no clamp.
- `src/main.rs:53-56` → row sampling is `row/(height-1)` with integer rows, so neither pole row is sampled.

**5. Sphere doc comments — CONFIRMED**
The style guide applies to `src/sphere.rs` and requires doc comments on public types and methods, `Sphere`, its fields and `Sphere::new` lack them while `Plane` and `Triangle` have them, and the base commit already lacked them, so this is pre-existing drift rather than B2 regression.
- `src/sphere.rs:9-18` → undocumented `Sphere` and `new`.
- `src/plane.rs:8-20`, `src/triangle.rs:8-21` → documented types and constructors.
- `DOCUMENTATION-STYLE-GUIDE.md:288` (also `:338`) → every public type/function/method has a doc comment.
- `git show e1293ef:src/sphere.rs` → base version has the same undocumented `Sphere`.

**6. Area 4, no findings — CONFIRMED**
`plane_axes` chooses the axis with the smallest absolute normal component, which for a unit normal is at most `1/√3`, so the cross magnitude is at least `√(1−1/3) = √(2/3) ≈ 0.816` and the axes can never be parallel; the zero-denominator guard, the `rem_euclid(1.0)` range and the `None` box are all as reported, and the one test pins the frozen axes and a negative wrapped coordinate (`v = -0.25 → 0.75`).
- `src/plane.rs:45-57` → helper selection and `u_axis = normal.cross(helper).unit()`, `v_axis = normal.cross(u_axis)`.
- `src/plane.rs:25,34-35,39-41` → `denominator == 0.0`, `rem_euclid(1.0)`, `None`.
- `src/plane.rs:64-74` → normal `(0,0,1)` gives `u=0.5`, `v=0.75`, proving `(0,1,0)` and `(-1,0,0)`.

**7. Triangle barycentric test would pass a weight swap — CONFIRMED**
The test ray hits `(0.25, 0.25)`, where `u == v`, so `assert_eq!(hit.u, 0.25)` and `assert_eq!(hit.v, 0.25)` cannot detect `u` and `v` being swapped.
- `src/triangle.rs:80` → ray origin `(0.25, 0.25, 0.0)`.
- `src/triangle.rs:88-89` → expected `hit.u == 0.25` and `hit.v == 0.25`.
- `src/triangle.rs:15-19` → `u` is the weight of `b`, `v` the weight of `c`, so the values should differ in the test.

**8. Untested triangle rejection paths — CONFIRMED**
No test exercises `determinant.abs() < 1e-8` (parallel ray), `v < 0.0`, `u + v > 1.0`, or a back-face triangle hit; the only other triangle test takes the `u`-range rejection, and the render tests assert no triangle behaviour at all.
- `src/triangle.rs:30-31,41,45` → the parallel, `v`/`u+v` and `t` rejections.
- `src/triangle.rs:73-101` → two tests: the in-triangle hit and a ray whose `u` is outside `0..=1`.
- `src/main.rs:95-107` → render tests assert only the centre pixel and the top-left pixel, neither of which is the triangle.

**9. `Aabb::hit` doc versus closed interval — CONFIRMED**
The doc says "`t` in `t_min..t_max`", but the code rejects only a strictly empty interval, so a hit exactly at `t == t_max` (and at `t == t_min`) is accepted, unlike every shape's strict `t >= t_max` rejection.
- `src/aabb.rs:20-21` → doc "with `t` in `t_min..t_max`".
- `src/aabb.rs:22-23,40` → `t_near = t_min`, `t_far = t_max`, reject only `t_near > t_far`.
- `src/triangle.rs:45` (and sphere/plane) → shapes reject `t >= t_max`, the inverse convention.

**10. Triangle's six componentwise min/max calls — CONFIRMED**
`Triangle::bounding_box` spells out three chained `.min` and three chained `.max` component expressions, and `Vec3` has no min/max helper; a one-caller helper would add public API for a single use, so calling it gold-plating is fair under §0.
- `src/triangle.rs:54-65` → six component expressions over `a`, `b`, `c`.
- `src/vec3.rs:12-36` → `new`, `dot`, `cross`, `length`, `unit` only.
- `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/BUILDING/REPO-RULES.md` §0 → do not add a second path or extra abstraction without need.

**11. Area 7, no findings — CONFIRMED**
`Vec3::cross` has four real callers, carries no `#[allow(dead_code)]` and no comment, and no inline cross product is duplicated anywhere else.
- `src/vec3.rs:21-27` → `cross` definition.
- `src/plane.rs:55-56` and `src/triangle.rs:27,39,49` → all callers.
- `git show 957bcf8 -- src/vec3.rs` → the old plan-naming comment and attribute were removed.

**12. Area 8, no findings — CONFIRMED**
`scene()` holds two spheres and the frozen triangle, the module list is alphabetical, every import is used, and `Plane` is never constructed (`Plane::new` appears only in `plane.rs`), so the module-level `allow(dead_code)` is needed for `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`; the same attribute already existed on the equally unused `mod rng` at the base commit, which was compiled successfully.
- `src/main.rs:3-13` → module list; `:17-22` → imports; `:36-46` → scene.
- `src/main.rs:6-7` and `:9-10` → `#[allow(dead_code)]` on `plane` and `rng`.
- `git show e1293ef:src/main.rs` → base had `#[allow(dead_code)] mod rng;`, confirming the pattern is required for an unused module's items.

**13. Aabb test as a duplicate §3a violation — WRONG**
It is not a true duplicate: the list test proves the guard wiring with a `Probe` and an origin outside the box on every axis, while the Aabb test exercises `Aabb::hit` directly with an origin inside the box, and it is the only direct coverage of the new `Aabb` primitive; different values and a different geometric case, so §3a's "already proven at another layer" does not apply.
- `src/aabb.rs:53-59` → box `[-1,1]³`, ray origin `(0,0,0)` inside it, hit/miss.
- `src/hittable.rs:110-124` → box `[5,6]×[5,6]×[-3,-2]`, both rays start outside it, and the object is a `Probe`, not an `Aabb` caller.
- `REPO-RULES.md` §3a → "a case already proven at another layer" is what must not be tested.

**14. Nearest-hit selection untested — CONFIRMED**
The list's only test uses a `Probe` that never returns a hit, and the two render tests' rays hit at most one object each, so replacing "nearest" with "last" (or "first") hit would leave all 11 tests green.
- `src/hittable.rs:66-80` → selection and `limit` narrowing.
- `src/hittable.rs:99-108` → `Probe::hit` always returns `None`; `:110-124` → only skip checks.
- `src/main.rs:38-44` and `:96-107` → the centre ray hits only the near sphere, the top-left ray hits nothing.

**15. RNG test can pass a constant generator — CONFIRMED, with a correction**
The test only compares two identically seeded streams, so a constant generator passes it; however requirement 6 asks for reproducibility ("the same options give the same bytes"), which a constant generator also satisfies, and `rng` is unused on plan-b, so requirement 6 is not "unpinned" by this test, only the property that the stream varies and depends on the seed is untouched.
- `src/rng.rs:29-36` → only `first.next_u64() == second.next_u64()` for seed 7.
- `src/main.rs:9-10` → `mod rng` is `allow(dead_code)` and no code calls `Rng`.
- `docs/requirements.md:19` → requirement 6 is the seeded-generator reproducibility rule in the Materials section.

**16. Full-image render tests — CONFIRMED**
Both render tests call `render(WIDTH, HEIGHT)` (200×100) and each asserts a single pixel, which contradicts the workspace rule that rendering tests check a few pixels of a small image and never a whole image.
- `src/main.rs:95-107` → two tests, each one `render(WIDTH, HEIGHT)` and one assertion.
- `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/repo-rules-domain.md:37` → "Rendering tests check a few pixels of a small image, never a whole image."

**17. Phase test-function accounting — CONFIRMED (the plan's claim is wrong)**
History shows B1 added one function and extended one, B2 added three, B2r added none and B3 added two, so six functions were added and the total is 11, while the plan's Z1 detail says B1 added three and eight were added overall.
- `phases/Z1-closing-survey-and-user-acceptance.md:39` and `:111` → "B1 added three" and "eight functions added".
- `git show 6eb43e0 -- src/sphere.rs` → adds only `a_ray_from_inside_the_sphere_flips_the_normal` and appends three asserts to `a_ray_through_the_center_hits_the_near_surface`.
- `git grep '#\[test\]'` at each commit → 5 base, 6 at B1, 6 at B2r, 9 at B2, 11 at B3; `done/B2-planes-and-triangles.md:37` correctly says B2 added three.

**18. `project.md:5` names `png.rs` and a command line absent from plan-b — CONFIRMED**
The shared repository map names `png.rs` and a command line that do not exist on branch `plan-b` (they exist on `plan-c`); it is not plan-b's to fix, because the file is workspace-shared and those entries belong to plan-c's accurate-for-merge description, while plan-b added only its own module names.
- `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md:5` → "`main.rs` (scene, render loop, output, command line), `png.rs` (PNG encoding)".
- `src/main.rs:86-89` → `fn main()` takes no arguments; no `png.rs` in plan-b `src/`.
- `git ls-tree -r --name-only plan-c` → `src/png.rs`; `git log --oneline plan-c -1` → `15bea28` adding the CLI.
- `done/B3-bounding-boxes.md:26` → plan-b's own edit to the map is the `aabb.rs` entry.

**19. `material.rs` missing from the map — CONFIRMED**
The same line omits `material.rs`, which plan-a has and plan-b does not, so the map is currently a partial union of parallel-plan modules.
- `AGENT-INSTRUCTIONS/LOCAL/project.md:5` → no `material.rs`.
- `/home/opc/projects/toy-raytracer-runs/run002/plan-a/src/material.rs` and `git ls-tree -r --name-only plan-a` → `src/material.rs` exists on plan-a.

**20. Requirement 10 wording gap for `HittableList::bounding_box` — WRONG**
There is no real requirement/intent gap: `HittableList` is the scene container, not one of the "objects" added to the scene, and the requirement explicitly exempts the one shape without a box (the infinite plane), so returning `None` for the list does not contradict item 10.
- `docs/requirements.md:29-30` → "Every object reports an axis-aligned bounding box ... An infinite plane has no box and is always tested."
- `src/hittable.rs:82-84` → `HittableList::bounding_box` returns `None`.
- `src/plane.rs:39-41` → the only shape returning `None`, exactly the stated exception.

**21. Base-commit public items lacking doc comments — CONFIRMED**
`Vec3` and its methods, `Ray`, `Rng` (except `next_f64`), `HittableList` and `add`, and `Sphere` all lack the doc comments the guide requires, and plan-b introduced none of them; the claim's list is also incomplete because `Camera` lacks a type doc.

- `src/vec3.rs:5-36`, `src/ray.rs:5-18`, `src/rng.rs:3-23`, `src/hittable.rs:53-63`, `src/sphere.rs:9-18`, `src/camera.rs:6-11` → undocumented public items.
- `git show e1293ef:<file>` → all of these predate plan-b; plan-b's new `Aabb`, `Plane`, `Triangle`, `HitRecord::new` and `Hittable::bounding_box` are documented.

## Missed findings

- **Shape boxes have no test at all.** `Sphere::bounding_box` (`src/sphere.rs:45-48`) and `Triangle::bounding_box` (`src/triangle.rs:53-66`) are never asserted; the only box test exercises `Aabb::hit` directly and the list guard through a `Probe` (`src/hittable.rs:105-107,110-124`). A box that is too small or built from the wrong corner would silently drop real hits in the scene while all 11 tests stay green, which bears directly on requirement 10 and is a larger correctness hole than the claimed nearest-hit gap.
- **The Z1 test-budget line also miscounts the total**, not only B1: `phases/Z1-closing-survey-and-user-acceptance.md:111` says eight functions were added across B1, B2 and B3, but the history gives six (5 → 11).

- **The documented zero-direction/NaN-on-face behaviour of `Aabb::hit` is untested.** `src/aabb.rs:31-32` states it, but the only test's rays have their zero-direction axes passing through the box centre, never a face, so the NaN-ignoring branch is never executed.

## Summary verdict

Most of the survey's findings check out: the comment-scope ambiguity (1), unused `Copy` (2), area 2's no-findings (3), the clamp reachability analysis (4), the missing sphere docs (5), area 4's geometry reasoning including the `√(2/3)` bound (6), the `u == v` test blind spot (7), the unexercised triangle rejections (8), the `Aabb` doc/interval mismatch (9), the six inline min/max calls (10), area 7 (11), area 8 (12), the nearest-hit coverage hole (14), the constant-generator weakness (15, though "requirement 6 unpinned" overstates it), the full-image render tests (16), the B1 test-count error (17, with B1 adding one and extending one, six added overall), the shared-map drift (18, 19) and the base-commit doc debt (21). Two claims are refuted: the Aabb test is not a §3a duplicate but the only direct test of a new primitive (13), and requirement 10's "every object" does not cover the scene container, so the list's `None` is not a wording/intent gap (20). The material findings that should reach the user are the untested shape bounding boxes and the nearest-hit/box-guard coverage holes, plus the B1/Z1 count error and the shared `project.md`/`full-plan.md` drift. I found no evidence of an operational or correctness defect in the current scene rendering.
